openingProblem.problem:
In February 1933 the League of Nations voted 42 to 1 against Japan's actions in Manchuria, and Japan simply walked out. Eight years later the United States, which was not a member of the League, cut off almost all trade with Japan, and within five months the two countries were at war.

Why did words fail to stop Japan in 1931–1933, and did economic pressure in 1941 restrain Japan or provoke it?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: which response did most to change Japan's course — the League, Chinese resistance, or US pressure? Give one reason.
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which source or fact changed or confirmed your judgement?

chunks.title: Why did the League of Nations fail to reverse the conquest of Manchuria?
chunks.body:
When Japan invaded Manchuria in September 1931, the League of Nations took up the dispute, and the United States, though not a member, offered support. On 5 October Secretary of State Stimson asked the League not to “relax its vigilance” and promised that the US would “endeavor to reinforce what the League does”; for the first time the US sat in on League Council meetings. But the world was in depression, and there was little support for economic sanctions.

The main responses were words. On 7 January 1932 Stimson told Japan and China that the US would not recognise any situation brought about against the Pact of Paris. On 11 March the League Assembly unanimously adopted the same principle of non-recognition. The League also sent a commission of enquiry under Lord Lytton, with members from Britain, the United States, Germany, Italy and France. It visited Tokyo on 29 February 1932, the day before Manchukuo was formally established.

The Lytton findings, announced on 2 October 1932, rejected Japan's claim of self-defence and refused to recognise Manchukuo, although they also blamed Chinese nationalism. Japan had already recognised Manchukuo in September. On 24 February 1933 the Assembly adopted the report by 42 votes to 1, with Siam abstaining; the Japanese delegate, Matsuoka, declared that Japan had reached “the limit” of cooperation, and his delegation left the hall. On 27 March Japan gave notice that it would leave the League.

This matters because the League had judged correctly but could not act. The United States agreed with the findings, yet in May 1933 Secretary of State Hull told the Senate that it would not use an arms embargo against Japan, because Japan made its own arms and could retaliate. Without sanctions or force, non-recognition had little effect. The crisis showed that the peace agreements of the 1920s could not stop a power determined to march forward, and Japan learned that aggression carried a low cost.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The League lacked the will and the means to enforce its judgement.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The League did reach a clear judgement against Japan and isolated it diplomatically.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Non-recognition was a moral response with little practical effect.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Manchukuo was never recognised by most states, so the principle had some lasting force.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the reasons why the League of Nations failed to reverse Japanese aggression in Manchuria.
To what extent was the Lytton report an effective response to the Manchurian crisis?
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about the US response to the Manchurian crisis.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The League failed because it could judge Japan but could not compel it.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 24 February 1933 the Assembly adopted the Lytton report 42 to 1; Japan walked out and gave notice to leave on 27 March.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because no major power would apply sanctions in the depression, and the US ruled out even an arms embargo, Japan lost nothing but its League membership.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the League did reach and publish a clear judgement, which most states upheld.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The failure lay in enforcement, not in judgement.

chunks.title: How did China respond: what did the Second United Front change?
chunks.body:
In 1931 Chiang Kai-shek's priority was the civil war against the Communists, and he did not resist in Manchuria. Pressure for a different policy grew. On 12 December 1936 two of his own generals, Chang Hsueh-liang (Zhang Xueliang) and Yang Hu-cheng, detained him at Xi'an and demanded a government including all factions and a united front against Japan. Most of the country rallied to Chiang, and his release on Christmas Day was greeted with enthusiasm.

In 1937 the two parties moved together. In June the Red troops were reported to be in the process of reorganisation into the national forces. After full-scale war began in July, the Communist Party issued a manifesto, reported in September, declaring that its aim was to resist invasion, that it supported Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles, and that it had cancelled its movement to overthrow the Kuomintang, stopped forcible land confiscation and abolished its soviet governments. The Red Army became the Eighth Route Army, under Chu Teh (Zhu De), and Communist forces south of the Yangzi became the New Fourth Army. Nationalist officials stressed that the Communists had “submerged themselves” and sworn allegiance to Chiang.

This matters because the united front allowed China to fight on after the loss of its great cities. Japan took Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan and Canton by November 1938, yet Chinese resistance continued, and by 1938 Chinese posters proclaimed that the longer the war lasted, the stronger China would become. Japan's hope of a quick victory, and of a new Chinese regime that would accept its terms, failed.

But the front was fragile. It functioned more as a non-aggression pact than a military alliance, and each side kept its own forces. In January 1941 Nationalist troops ambushed and defeated New Fourth Army units in southern Anhui. The Second United Front therefore strengthened China's resistance by ending the civil war for a time, but it did not create a united state, and tension between the two parties continued throughout the war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The united front kept China fighting after the fall of its main cities.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: China also depended on foreign aid and on its vast interior, not only on unity.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The front was fragile and limited.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Despite clashes such as January 1941, neither party made peace with Japan.

useItInAnEssay.explain: Because both parties now fought Japan, China could continue the war after losing Shanghai, Nanjing and Wuhan, which defeated Japan's hope of a quick victory.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the front functioned more as a non-aggression pact, and in January 1941 Nationalist troops attacked the New Fourth Army.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The front was essential to China's survival but never produced real unity.

chunks.title: How effective were US responses to Japanese aggression, 1937–1940?
chunks.body:
Before 1937 most US officials believed the United States had no vital interests in China worth a war with Japan. When full-scale war began, Washington responded first with principles. On 16 July 1937 Hull issued a statement calling for peace, self-restraint and respect for treaties. On 5 October Roosevelt warned in Chicago that “the epidemic of world lawlessness is spreading” and spoke of a “quarantine”, though he named no country and stressed that the US was “determined to keep out of war”. The next day the League condemned Japan's action as a breach of its treaty obligations, and in November the US joined 18 other nations at a conference in Brussels, which Japan refused to attend.

The Panay incident tested these words. On 12 December 1937 Japanese aircraft sank the US gunboat Panay on the Yangtze, killing three. The US demanded regret, compensation and guarantees; Japan apologised on 14 December, claiming a mistake caused by poor visibility, and later paid in full. The American public overwhelmingly approved of this settlement, which showed its wish to stay out of war.

This matters because US policy shifted gradually from words to economic measures. From July 1938 a “moral embargo” discouraged the sale of aircraft to Japan, and credit was informally discouraged. In July 1939 the US gave notice to end the 1911 commercial treaty, which removed the legal obstacle to an embargo. The Export Control Act of July 1940 allowed licences for aviation gasoline and machine tools to be refused, and a scrap iron and steel embargo took effect on 16 October 1940. When Japan's ambassador called it an “unfriendly act”, Hull replied that Japan was “bent on the conquest by force of all worthwhile territory in the Pacific Ocean area”.

These measures did not stop Japanese expansion: Japan took Wuhan and Canton in 1938 and entered Indochina in 1940. Britain even closed the Burma Road, China's supply route, for three months in 1940. But US pressure made Japan's need for secure resources more urgent, which helps explain the move south.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Moral appeals and conferences did not change Japanese policy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: They kept the US out of war, which was what most Americans wanted.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic measures grew from 1938 but came too slowly to stop expansion.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The measures cut Japan's supplies and pushed it to seek resources elsewhere, which raised the risk of war.

useItInAnEssay.claim: US responses in 1937–1940 were too limited to stop Japanese expansion.
useItInAnEssay.prove: After the Panay was sunk in December 1937 the US accepted an apology and indemnity, and only in October 1940 did a scrap embargo take effect.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because public opinion wanted to avoid war, Washington moved slowly from words to economic pressure, which left Japan free to expand in China and into Indochina.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the measures of 1939–1940 began to cut Japan's supplies and prepared the ground for the freeze of 1941.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The responses were cautious and ineffective as a deterrent, though they shaped Japan's later choices.

chunks.title: Did US pressure in 1941 restrain Japan or push it to war?
chunks.body:
By 1941 the United States had become the decisive outside power in the Far East. It was giving China credits and, under Lend-Lease, war supplies, while slowly restricting what Japan could buy. Oil was the hardest question. In September 1940 Ambassador Grew had warned that drastic embargoes on products such as oil would be read in Japan as sanctions and that retaliation “might and probably would follow”.

Roosevelt explained his oil policy directly to Ambassador Nomura on 24 July 1941. For more than two years, he said, oil had been allowed to go to Japan because cutting it off would have given Japan a pretext to move on the Netherlands East Indies, and an attack there would bring war with the Dutch and the British. But Japan was now moving into southern Indochina. Two days later, on 26 July, the President froze Japanese assets in the United States, and at Chiang Kai-shek's request froze Chinese assets too, to help China. Trade between the United States and Japan very soon virtually stopped.

This matters because the freeze changed the nature of the crisis. Japan could either accept American terms or seize resources by force. Talks continued, but on 26 November 1941 Hull's proposal required Japan to withdraw all its forces from China and Indochina. Japan's answer, handed over on 7 December after the attack on Pearl Harbor had begun, condemned the freezing order and described economic pressure as “at times more inhumane than military pressure”.

US pressure therefore did not restrain Japan; it narrowed Japan's choices. Yet the pressure was a response to Japan's own expansion, and the US had held back on oil for two years precisely to avoid provoking a southward move. Historians must weigh whether economic sanctions caused the war or whether Japan's refusal to leave China made war likely whatever the US did.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The freeze of July 1941 left Japan choosing between retreat and war.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The freeze followed Japan's own move into southern Indochina.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The US had tried to avoid provoking Japan by allowing oil exports for two years.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Critics in the US argued that this fed Japan's war in China.

useItInAnEssay.claim: US economic pressure narrowed Japan's choices but did not by itself cause the war.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 26 July 1941 Roosevelt froze Japanese assets and trade soon virtually stopped; on 26 November Hull demanded withdrawal from China and Indochina.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because Japan's leaders would not leave China, the freeze left them a choice between shortages and seizing resources by force.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the freeze responded to Japan's move into southern Indochina, and Roosevelt had held back on oil for two years to keep peace.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economic pressure was a trigger; Japan's refusal to give up its conquests was the deeper cause.

sourceSets.focus: The League of Nations and the Lytton report, 1931–1933

provenance.creator: Gilbert, US Consul at Geneva
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State reporting the special Assembly of the League of Nations
provenance.contextNote: The Assembly was voting on a report based on the findings of the League's Lytton Commission. Words in square brackets are corrections printed in the published record or added for sense.

sources.text: 6. … The Assembly proceeded to a roll call vote with the following result: (1) Number of states voting 44; (2) number of states voting affirmatively (including all 12 Council members other [than] the parties to the dispute) and including China 42; (3) number of states voting negatively 1, Japan; (4) states present but abstaining 1, Siam … 8. Matsuoka made a “final declaration” in which he expressed the profound [regret] and disappointment of the Japanese delegation at the result of the Assembly's vote. He concluded in the following terms: “The Japanese now find themselves compelled to conclude that Japan and the other members of the League entertain different views on the manner to achieve peace in the Far East and the Japanese Government are obliged to feel that they have now reached the limit of their endeavors to cooperate with the League of Nations in reference to the Sino-Japanese differences.” … Immediately following the end of Matsuoka's declaration however the entire Japanese delegation left the Assembly room.

provenance.creator: Agence Meurisse, a French press photo agency
provenance.contextNote: Members of the League of Nations commission of enquiry (the Lytton Commission) with the Japanese Prime Minister, Inukai Tsuyoshi (front row, centre), at the Prime Minister's official residence in Tokyo. Lord Lytton stands front left.

provenance.creator: Henry L. Stimson, US Secretary of State
provenance.sourceType: letter to the Secretary General of the League of Nations, released to the press

sources.text: In the situation which has developed out of the controversy between China and Japan, the purpose of the United States has coincided in general with that of the League of Nations, the common objective being maintenance of peace and settlement of international disputes by pacific means. In pursuance of that objective, while the League of Nations has been exercising jurisdiction over a controversy between two of its members, the Government of the United States has endeavored to give support, reserving to itself independence of judgment with regard to method and scope, to the efforts of the League on behalf of peace. The findings of fact arrived at by the League and the understanding of the facts derived by the American Government from reports made to it by its own representatives are in substantial accord. … With those conclusions the American Government is in general accord. In their affirmations respectively of the principle of non-recognition and their attitude in regard thereto the League and the United States are on common ground.

provenance.creator: Cordell Hull, US Secretary of State
provenance.sourceType: memorandum presented to the Committee on Foreign Relations of the US Senate
provenance.contextNote: The Senate was considering a resolution allowing the President to ban arms exports to countries at war.

sources.text: It has never been the intention and is not now the intention of this Government to use the authority which would be conferred upon the Executive by this Resolution as a means of restoring peace between China and Japan. An embargo on arms and munitions of war would not be an effective means of restoring peace in this case. Japan is an important producer of arms and munitions of war. … China is dependent upon her importation of these commodities. … An embargo directed against Japan alone would probably result in a Japanese blockade of Chinese ports, in the seizure by the Japanese of arms and munitions intended for China … we would not under any circumstances agree to participate in an international embargo of this kind unless we had secured substantial guarantees from the governments of all of the great powers which would ensure us against the effects of any retaliatory measures which the Japanese might undertake.

questions.text: According to Source A, what happened at the League Assembly on 24 February 1933?

points: 42 states voted for the report, including China.
Japan alone voted against it.
Siam abstained.
Matsuoka declared that Japan had reached the limit of its cooperation with the League.
The whole Japanese delegation left the Assembly room.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the League's response to the Manchurian crisis?

points: The League sent a senior international commission, with members from several powers, to investigate.
The commission worked through formal meetings with the Japanese government, relying on enquiry and diplomacy rather than pressure.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying international responses to the Manchurian crisis.

points: Value (origin): the US Secretary of State's formal reply to the League sets out the official US position.
Value (content): it shows that the US agreed with the League's findings and shared the principle of non-recognition, though it was not a member.
Limitation (purpose): written for publication, so it stresses agreement and says nothing about whether the US would support sanctions.
Limitation (content): it gives the US view only; it cannot show how other League members or Japan responded.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources C and D reveal about the US response to Japanese aggression in Manchuria.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources show that the US agreed with the League's judgement: Source C says the US is “in general accord” with the League's conclusions, and Source D that it “concurs in general in the findings” placing responsibility on Japan.
Both also show the US keeping its independence: C reserves “independence of judgment with regard to method and scope”, and D sets conditions before joining any embargo.
However, Source C offers only moral support and the principle of non-recognition, while Source D explicitly rules out using an arms embargo to restore peace between China and Japan.
Source C speaks to the League and world opinion, whereas Source D speaks to the Senate and stresses the risk of Japanese retaliation against the US.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the reasons why the League of Nations failed to reverse Japanese aggression in Manchuria between 1931 and 1933.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: The League failed because it could judge Japan but no power was willing to enforce its judgement.

Sources B and A show the League's method: an international commission of enquiry, followed by a report adopted 42 to 1. The Lytton findings, announced on 2 October 1932, rejected Japan's claim of self-defence.
But Japan had already recognised Manchukuo in September 1932, and Source A shows its response to the vote: the delegation simply left. Japan gave notice to leave the League on 27 March 1933.

Sources C and D explain the weakness: the US agreed with the findings but offered only non-recognition, and refused even an arms embargo for fear of retaliation. In the depression there was little support for economic sanctions.
The League's failure lay in enforcement rather than judgement: without sanctions, Japan lost nothing but its membership.

sourceSets.focus: The Xi'an incident and the Second United Front, 1936–1937

provenance.creator: Johnson, US Ambassador in China
provenance.sourceType: despatch to the US Secretary of State reviewing the second half of 1936, sent from Peiping
provenance.contextNote: Sian is Xi'an. Chang Hsueh-liang is Zhang Xueliang.

sources.text: On December 12 General Chang Hsueh-liang and General Yang Hu-cheng, the Pacification Commissioner of Shensi, revolted against Nanking and forcibly detained Chiang Kai-shek and other important Central Government officials who were in Sian with the Generalissimo. The leaders of the rebellion issued a statement demanding a reorganization of the Government to include all factions, presumably even the Communists, and for a united front against Japan. Shensi and Kansu responded to the plea, but the rest of the country loudly proclaimed its adherence to the Generalissimo and voiced the bitterest contempt for Chang Hsueh-liang and the revolt. The Generalissimo's release on Christmas day was greeted with enthusiasm throughout the country which had again become more closely knit through common patriotic zeal. A very regrettable aftermath of the Sian coup was the reported alliance between the mutineers and the communists who had been concentrated for some time in the vicinity of Sian.

provenance.creator: Xin Ke, Chinese artist
provenance.sourceType: poster produced for the China branch of the International Anti-Aggression Association
provenance.contextNote: The title reads: “The more I fight, the stronger I become; the more the enemy fights, the weaker he becomes.” A Chinese soldier, with aircraft behind him, towers over caricatures of Japanese soldiers in flames.

provenance.creator: Josselyn, US Consul General at Hankow
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State
provenance.contextNote: Full-scale war between Japan and China had begun in July 1937.

sources.text: Hankow vernacular press has published manifesto reported issued by Central Committee of Chinese Communist Party in Shensi declaring that Communist Party objectives are to resist invasion, bring about popular government and improve welfare of people. Communist Party will now cooperate with whole nation in furthering these objectives. Party declared its support of three principles of Sun Yat Sen; declares it has cancelled all movements for overthrowing political power of Kuomintang including forcible confiscation of land and abolished all existing Soviet governments. The Red Army is reorganized into National Revolutional Army under command of Military Council of the National Government. Army is awaiting orders to undertake duty at the front.

provenance.creator: Johnson, US Ambassador in China
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State, sent from Nanking
provenance.contextNote: “Official sources” means the Nationalist government. Chu Teh is Zhu De.

sources.text: Official sources confirm press reports from Sian that Military Affairs Commission has appointed Chu Teh, Commander and Peng Teh Hui, Vice Commander of the Chinese Communist forces in the northwest which have been reorganized into Government forces as the Eighth Route Army. According to official sources the cooperation of these forces with Government forces in present hostilities can not be described as formation of “popular front” because the Communists have submerged themselves in that they have promised not to engage in Communist propaganda, have relinquished the class struggle, have no longer their Communist character and Chu Teh and Peng have sworn their allegiance and obedience to Chiang Kai-shek.

questions.text: According to Source A, how did China react to the Xi'an (Sian) incident?

points: Shensi and Kansu supported the rebels' plea.
The rest of the country proclaimed its loyalty to Chiang and showed contempt for Chang Hsueh-liang.
Chiang's release on Christmas Day was greeted with enthusiasm.
The country became “more closely knit through common patriotic zeal”.

questions.text: What is the message of Source B?

points: China will grow stronger the longer the war goes on, while Japan will grow weaker.
Chinese soldiers, backed by modern aircraft, will overcome the Japanese.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying the Second United Front.

points: Value (origin): a US consul's report written at the time from Hankow, where the manifesto was published.
Value (content): it lists the Communist Party's public terms: support for Sun Yat-sen's principles, no more attempts to overthrow the Kuomintang, and the Red Army under national command.
Limitation (origin): it summarises a manifesto “reported” in the local press, so it is second-hand and abbreviated.
Limitation (purpose): a brief news telegram to Washington; it cannot show whether the Communists meant or kept these promises.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources C and D reveal about the terms of cooperation between the Communists and the Nationalists.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources agree that the Communist army was placed under the national government: Source C says the Red Army was reorganised “under command of Military Council of the National Government”, and Source D that it became the Eighth Route Army.
Both also report that the Communists gave up revolutionary aims: C mentions the end of “forcible confiscation of land” and of soviet governments, and D says they “relinquished the class struggle”.

However, Source C presents a partnership, with the Party cooperating “with whole nation” for shared objectives, while Source D presents submission: the Communists “have submerged themselves” and “have no longer their Communist character”.
Source C reports the Communists' own manifesto, whereas Source D reports Nationalist “official sources”, which explains the different emphasis.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent did the Second United Front strengthen Chinese resistance to Japan between 1937 and 1941?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: The Second United Front greatly strengthened Chinese resistance by suspending the civil war, but it remained a fragile truce rather than a true alliance.

Source A shows the pressure for unity after the Xi'an incident of December 1936, and Sources C and D show its terms in September 1937: the Red Army became the Eighth Route Army under the National Government.

This allowed China to keep fighting after losing Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan and Canton by 1938, and Source B reflects the confidence that a long war favoured China, which defeated Japan's hope of a quick victory.

However, the front worked more as a non-aggression pact; Source D shows the Nationalists treating it as Communist submission, and in January 1941 Nationalist troops ambushed New Fourth Army units in southern Anhui.
The front strengthened resistance to a large extent by preventing a Chinese collapse, but it never ended the rivalry between the two parties.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.

provenance.creator: Roosevelt, US President
provenance.contextNote: Japan's war in China had begun in July 1937. The address does not name any country.

sources.text: The peace-loving nations must make a concerted effort in opposition to those violations of treaties and those ignorings of humane instincts which today are creating a state of international anarchy and instability from which there is no escape through mere isolation or neutrality. … It seems to be unfortunately true that the epidemic of world lawlessness is spreading. When an epidemic of physical disease starts to spread, the community approves and joins in a quarantine of the patients in order to protect the health of the community against the spread of the disease. It is my determination to pursue a policy of peace and to adopt every practicable measure to avoid involvement in war. … War is a contagion, whether it be declared or undeclared. … We are determined to keep out of war, yet we cannot insure ourselves against the disastrous effects of war and the danger of involvement.

provenance.creator: US Navy
provenance.contextNote: The US Navy river gunboat Panay sinking in the Yangtze River between Nanking and Wuhu after an attack by Japanese aircraft. A US flag is spread across the awnings on deck; a motor boat carries survivors away.

provenance.creator: Hirota Kōki, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
provenance.sourceType: note to the US Ambassador, Joseph Grew (informal translation by the Japanese Foreign Office)

sources.text: From the reports subsequently received from our representatives in China, it has been established that the Japanese naval air force, acting upon information that the Chinese troops fleeing from Nanking were going up the river in steamers, took off to pursue them, and discovered such vessels at the above-mentioned point. Owing to poor visibility, however, the aircraft, although they descended to fairly low altitudes, were unable to discern any mark to show that any one of them was an American ship or man-of-war. … While it is clear, in the light of the above circumstances, that the present incident was entirely due to a mistake, the Japanese Government regret most profoundly that it has caused damages to the United States man-of-war and ships and casualties among those on board, and desire to present hereby sincere apologies. The Japanese Government will make indemnifications for all the losses and will deal appropriately with those responsible for the incident.

provenance.creator: Cordell Hull, US Secretary of State
provenance.sourceType: memorandum of a conversation with the Japanese Ambassador, Horinouchi
provenance.contextNote: The Ambassador had protested against the US embargo on exports of iron and steel scrap.

sources.text: I said that it was really amazing for the Government of Japan, which has been violating in the most aggravating manner valuable American rights and interests throughout most of China, and is doing so in many instances every day, to question the fullest privilege of this Government from every standpoint to impose the proposed scrap iron and steel embargo, and that to go still further and call it an unfriendly act was still more amazing in the light of the conduct of the Japanese Government in disregarding all law, treaty obligations and other rights and privileges and the safety of Americans while it proceeded at the same time to seize territory by force to an ever-increasing extent. … I went on to say that we have stood for law and order and treaty observance and justice along with genuine friendliness between our two countries; that it was clear now, however, that those who are dominating the external policies of Japan are, as we here have believed for some years, bent on the conquest by force of all worthwhile territory in the Pacific Ocean area without limit as to extent in the South …

questions.text: According to Source A, what should peace-loving nations do about world lawlessness?

points: Make a concerted effort against violations of treaties.
Recognise that isolation or neutrality offers no escape.
Treat lawlessness like an epidemic and join in a “quarantine”.
Act while still trying to keep out of war.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the Panay incident?

points: The US gunboat was clearly marked with a large US flag, yet it was sunk.
The attack forced the crew to abandon ship, with survivors taken off by boat.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying relations between Japan and the United States after 1937.

points: Value (origin): the Japanese Foreign Minister's official note shows Japan's formal response to the crisis.
Value (content): it shows Japan offering apologies, compensation and punishment, which reveals that Japan wished to avoid a break with the US in 1937.
Limitation (purpose): written to calm the US and limit damage, so its claim that the sinking was “entirely due to a mistake” caused by poor visibility is self-serving.
Limitation (content): it gives no independent evidence; the photograph in Source B shows a large US flag on the ship.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about the US attitude to aggression in East Asia.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources condemn the breaking of treaties and law: Source A attacks “violations of treaties”, and Source D accuses Japan of “disregarding all law, treaty obligations”.
Both present the US as standing for peace and order: A speaks of “a policy of peace”, and D of US support for “law and order and treaty observance and justice”.

However, Source A names no country and calls only for a concerted moral effort while keeping out of war, whereas Source D accuses Japan directly of seeking “the conquest by force of all worthwhile territory in the Pacific Ocean area”.
Source A offers no concrete measure, while Source D defends a specific economic weapon, the scrap iron and steel embargo, showing a shift from words to action between 1937 and 1940.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the effectiveness of US responses to Japanese expansion between 1937 and 1940.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: US responses in 1937–1940 were largely ineffective in stopping Japanese expansion, though they began to restrict Japan's supplies.
Source A shows the first response: moral appeal and a “quarantine” image, with no concrete measure; the Brussels Conference of November 1937, which Japan refused to attend, achieved nothing.
Sources B and C show the limits of US firmness: after the Panay was sunk the US accepted Japan's apology and indemnity, and Americans overwhelmingly approved because they wanted to stay out of war.

Pressure grew slowly: a moral embargo on aircraft in 1938, notice to end the commercial treaty in July 1939, and, as Source D shows, a scrap iron and steel embargo by October 1940. Yet Japan took Wuhan and Canton in 1938 and entered Indochina in 1940.
The responses avoided war but did not deter Japan; by restricting supplies they increased Japan's urge to secure resources further south.

sourceSets.focus: US initiatives and rising tension with Japan, 1941

provenance.creator: Welles, Acting US Secretary of State
provenance.sourceType: memorandum of President Roosevelt's meeting with the Japanese Ambassador, Admiral Nomura, at the White House
provenance.contextNote: Japanese troops were moving into southern French Indochina.

sources.text: The President said, referring to a talk which he had made this morning to a home defense group under the leadership of Mayor LaGuardia, that for more than two years the United States had been permitting oil to be exported from the United States to Japan. He said that this had been done because of the realization on the part of the United States that if these oil supplies had been shut off or restricted the Japanese Government and people would have been furnished with an incentive or a pretext for moving down upon the Netherlands East Indies in order to assure themselves of a greater oil supply than that which, under present conditions, they were able to obtain. … The President said that if Japan attempted to seize oil supplies by force in the Netherlands East Indies, the Dutch would, without the shadow of a doubt, resist, the British would immediately come to their assistance, war would then result between Japan, the British and the Dutch, and, in view of our own policy of assisting Great Britain, an exceedingly serious situation would immediately result.

provenance.creator: Photographer of the Japanese newspaper Mainichi Shimbun
provenance.contextNote: The US Secretary of State, Cordell Hull (centre), walks with the Japanese Ambassador, Admiral Nomura Kichisaburō (left), and the special envoy Kurusu Saburō (right) to a meeting with President Roosevelt at the White House.

sources.text: In view of the unlimited national emergency declared by the President, he issued, on July 26, an Executive order freezing Japanese assets in the United States in the same manner in which assets of various European countries were frozen on June 14, 1941. This measure, in effect, brings all financial and import and export trade transactions in which Japanese interests are involved under the control of the Government and imposes criminal penalties for violation of the order. … At the specific request of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, and for the purpose of helping the Chinese Government, the President has, at the same time, extended the freezing control to Chinese assets in the United States. … The inclusion of China in the Executive Order, in accordance with the wishes of the Chinese Government, is a continuation of this Government's policy of assisting China.

provenance.creator: Japanese Government
provenance.sourceType: memorandum handed to the US Secretary of State by Ambassador Nomura and Mr Kurusu
provenance.contextNote: The memorandum was handed over about an hour after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor had begun.

sources.text: Furthermore, when Japan in accordance with its protocol with France took measures of joint defence of French Indo-China, both American and British Governments, willfully misinterpreting it as a threat to their own possessions, and inducing the Netherlands Government to follow suit, they enforced the assets freezing order, thus severing economic relations with Japan. While manifesting thus an obviously hostile attitude, these countries have strengthened their military preparations perfecting an encirclement of Japan, and have brought about a situation which endangers the very existence of the Empire. … 3. Whereas the American Government, under the principles it rigidly upholds, objects to settle international issues through military pressure, it is exercising in conjunction with Great Britain and other nations pressure by economic power. Recourse to such pressure as a means of dealing with international relations should be condemned as it is at times more inhumane than military pressure.

questions.text: According to Source A, why had the United States allowed oil exports to Japan?

points: Cutting off oil would give Japan an incentive or pretext to move on the Netherlands East Indies.
Japan would then try to secure a greater oil supply by force.
The Dutch would resist and the British would help them, so war would follow.
Because the US was assisting Britain, the US itself would face an exceedingly serious situation.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about US–Japanese relations in November 1941?

points: Negotiations were still taking place at the highest level, with the President.
Japan had sent a special envoy, showing the talks were urgent and serious.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying US economic measures against Japan in 1941.

points: Value (origin): an official White House statement issued on the day of the freeze gives the exact terms of the measure.
Value (content): it shows that the freeze brought all trade with Japanese interests under government control and that it was linked to aid for China.
Limitation (purpose): a public announcement that presents the measure as defensive and does not mention oil or the risk of war.
Limitation (content): it shows US intentions on 26 July, not the effect of the freeze, which very soon stopped nearly all trade.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about US economic pressure on Japan in 1941.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources link economic measures to the danger of war: Source A explains that cutting off oil could lead Japan to seize the Netherlands East Indies, and Source D says the freeze created “a situation which endangers the very existence of the Empire”.

Both mention the Netherlands and Britain as involved in the crisis: A predicts that the Dutch would resist and the British help them, and D accuses the US of “inducing the Netherlands Government to follow suit”.

However, Source A presents the US as having held back on oil for two years to preserve peace, while Source D presents US economic pressure as hostile, part of an “encirclement”, and “more inhumane than military pressure”.
Source A treats Japanese expansion as the threat, whereas Source D treats Japan's move into Indochina as “joint defence” and blames the West.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent was US economic pressure responsible for the outbreak of war between Japan and the United States in December 1941?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: US economic pressure was an important cause because it narrowed Japan's choices, but Japan's refusal to give up its conquests in China was the deeper cause.

Source A shows that the US had avoided an oil embargo for two years for fear of provoking Japan; the freeze in Source C came only after Japan moved into southern Indochina, and trade then virtually stopped.
Source D shows that Japan's leaders blamed the freeze and economic “encirclement” for the war, and Grew had warned in September 1940 that oil embargoes would provoke retaliation.

However, Source B shows that talks were still going on in November; they failed because Hull's proposal of 26 November 1941 required Japan to withdraw all forces from China and Indochina, which Japan would not accept.
Economic pressure turned tension into crisis, but war came because Japan chose to fight rather than give up its expansion.
